source.title: Challenge: Hand coding weights for efficient sequence memorisation

record.file_problem: The supplied post is readable, but some equations, table values, and figure labels are missing or garbled in the web text.
record.tranche_reason: It trains one-layer toy transformers on random input-to-label mappings and reports memorization capacity, extending the random-label fitting result to a sequence task and toy architectures.
record.gate_note: The post reports its own random-label sequence experiments. Results it cites from prior work and commenters' experiments are not rows. The architecture comparison tables and scaling plots contain missing values in the supplied text, so only stated outcomes are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own Adam-trained networks achieving zero training classification error on random two-token-to-label mappings, extending random-label fitting to toy sequence models. Its hand-coded constructions are separate from this evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors find that trained toy models memorize random sequence mappings and that the MLP contributes most to capacity. Their central contribution is a hand-coded construction: it approximately matches trained-model scaling at 90% accuracy while storing roughly 9.7 times fewer facts, falls increasingly behind at perfect accuracy, and improves with a trained readout. They caution that measured capacity also reflects trainability.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses random two-token sequence-to-label mappings and one-layer toy transformers or a stripped-down MLP, rather than image-classification networks. It varies architecture and measures maximum memorized facts.
record.method_sensitivity: Capacity varies with architecture: MLP presence has the largest reported effect; mixing choice and norms also affect results. Learned attention results are described as least stable across repeated runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Hand-coded and hybrid constructions differ from fully trained models in storage efficiency and weight or activation patterns.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit weight constructions can approach the random-association storage capacity of fully trained toy models.

record.problems: The study uses toy sequence data rather than images and does not report test error or true-label generalization. Key dimensions, table values, and figure datapoints are missing in the supplied web text. The authors note that observed capacity can reflect trainability rather than theoretical architecture capacity, and report stability differences across architecture variants.
record.rows_left_out: The post's hand-coded and hybrid capacity results compare constructed weights with trained weights, but do not independently add a random-label fitting result beyond the trained-model rows. Figure-only numeric datapoints, including separate absolute capacities and full/simple scaling exponents, could not be recovered from the supplied text. Commenter experiments and cited studies are excluded.

untested.parts: Held-out error at chance and fitting random versus meaningful labels with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters are not tested. Results concern toy sequence models, with full-batch Adam and a conditional learning-rate schedule.
No training-time comparison with true labels or corruption-fraction sweep.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
No mixed signal/noise labels, corruption-fraction sweep, or test-error trajectory.
No controlled weight-decay, dropout, or augmentation comparison, and no true-label generalization experiment. Using Adam without weight decay alone does not test this version.
No comparison of learning real patterns before memorizing noisy labels.

missing.what: A readable absolute perfect-fitting result: without MLP or norms, dual embedding and uniform attention each fit 208 random facts in all four repeated searches; learned attention fits 208 in two searches and slightly different counts in the others.

The MLP-present, norms-on, residual-free, bias-free ReLU configuration has unusually low perfect-fitting capacity across all mixing choices. Removing norms, adding MLP bias, or switching to GELU restores the usual capacity range. This documents architecture sensitivity, without establishing absence of random-label fitting.
missing.locator: Results, final paragraph; Appendix B, outlier discussion; footnote 15

record.verdict_notes: Missing test-error and true-label comparisons are untested components, not grounds for limits_scope. Lower capacity across architectures and the 90% evaluation threshold likewise do not establish failure of perfect fitting at the capacities measured elsewhere. Labels exclude hand-coded results and commenter experiments. Labels are balanced across output classes rather than sampled independently, and the reported main architecture comparisons use success in any of 11 initializations.

versions.untested_parts: The task uses random labels on two-token sequences, not training images; it does not report test error or compare true-label generalization against random-label training.
Training time or epochs for random labels versus true labels and corruption-rate effects on convergence are not compared.
Shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
There is no sweep over fractions of corrupted labels or test-error measurement.
The post does not test weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation in relation to random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The post does not compare learning dynamics for real versus noisy or random labels.

rows.measure: Maximum number of randomly labeled facts learned
rows.value: Adding an MLP block lets the network learn 324 - 794 (60% - 373%) more facts; other stated architecture effects are recorded separately in R2.
rows.uncertainty: 11 random initializations per tested fact count; four repeated binary searches; main analysis uses the 'Any' criterion.
rows.locator: Results; Appendix B, Table B.3 and accompanying text
rows.note: The post reports aggregate differences across architecture comparisons, not an absolute capacity for this model. This is evidence of fitting random labels in the stated toy task.
rows.check: The subject is a collection of architecture variants, not exclusively the full transformer. The reported value is a capacity difference, but capacity explicitly requires every training label to be correct. The comparisons exclude the anomalous norms-on, bias-free, residual-free ReLU configuration.
